newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Gold - Physical demand retreats on price rise. [CORRECTED 5:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold - Physical demand retreats on price rise. [CORRECTED 5:55 GMT]

text.p: Asian demand for physical gold eased on Friday following a steep rise in spot gold prices in New York overnight, and buying would likely be reined in until prices dropped again, Hong Kong and Singapore dealers said.
"Demand has dropped today," said a gold dealer at a European bullion firm in Hong Kong, noting that the big jewellery houses and the retail sector were holding back on their gold purchases.
"Physical buyers are going to hold off for the next few days with prices at these levels," another dealer in a Singapore-based bank said.
Hong Kong gold opened unchanged from New York's close of $350.40/90 an ounce. Traders expected prices to firm during the day, but activity was expected to be sluggish.
Hong Kong bullion ended at $344.90/345.40 an ounce on Thursday.

Heavy shortcovering in New York overnight drove spot gold prices up, helped by news on Thursday that South African Reserve Bank governor, Chris Stals, said he did not expect last year's Belgian and Dutch central bank gold sales to be followed by other central bank gold sales.
Gold prices fell to three year lows last week (corrects from year) due partly to fears of further central bank sales. But short covering this week has lifted the metal.
Dealers in Hong Kong and Singapore said gold has the potential to test $355-$357 an ounce, although such gains, if sustained, could further discourage strong purchases.
"Buyers don't mind picking up gold in the $340s, but they will change their minds if the price settles in the $350s," a senior trader for a North American bank in Singapore said.
Traders said strong buying of the yellow metal was more likely to kick in at $348-$349 an ounce.

Buying around Southeast Asia has been heavy in the past few weeks, traders said. But the weaker rupiah in Indonesia will now discourage buying there while the higher international price would sideline other players, the Singapore sources said.
"It'll be more expensive now for Indonesian buyers to buy gold so the volume of buying there may slow down for a while," one trader said.
Premiums remained steady at 120-140 U.S. cents an ounce over spot London prices, Singapore dealers said, although premiums as high as 170 U.S. cents were seen in Hong Kong.
"The premiums are strong because we can still see some demand out there, but that may not last long," one bank trader said.
Dealers said the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on Wednesday had already been ignored by the market and they expected no impact on trade during China's six-day mourning period.
